Images that carry meaning, such as a chart, need a label that gives the meaning, not the appearance: "Steps for the last seven days, rising", not "bar chart". `accessibilityElement(children: .combine)` merges the children of a row into one element, which saves the user many swipes.
Dynamic Type: let the user choose the text size

In Settings, people can make text much larger, and some choose the largest accessibility sizes. If your app uses the built-in text styles, such as `.body`, `.headline` and `.title`, the text scales automatically. If you set a fixed point size with `.font(.system(size: 14))`, it does not. Prefer styles. When you need a custom size, use `@ScaledMetric` so spacing and icons grow with the text.

The example switches from a row to a column at the accessibility sizes, using `AnyLayout`. A row that fits at the normal size can push text off the screen at the largest size. Never truncate important text to a single line with `.lineLimit(1)` unless you are sure it still makes sense.
Colour, contrast and motion

items: **Do not rely on colour alone.** In the quiz project, the right answer shows a check mark as well as green, because some people cannot tell red from green.

**Contrast**: text needs enough difference from its background. WCAG, the common web guideline, suggests a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text. System colours such as `.primary` and `.secondary` adapt to light and dark mode and to the Increase Contrast setting.
**Reduce Motion**: some users feel ill from large animations. Read `@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion)` and use a simple fade or no animation when it is on.
**Touch targets**: make tappable things at least about 44 by 44 points, which is Apple's design guidance.
**Captions and transcripts**: video and audio need captions or a text alternative.

content.text: Testing accessibility

items: Run the app in the Simulator, open **Xcode > Open Developer Tool > Accessibility Inspector**, point it at your app and run the audit. It lists missing labels and small targets.
Turn on **VoiceOver** on a real iPhone (Settings > Accessibility) and use the app with your eyes closed for two minutes. Nothing teaches faster.
Preview several text sizes in Xcode with `.environment(\.dynamicTypeSize, .accessibility3)` on your previews.
Turn on Bold Text, Increase Contrast and Reduce Motion in Settings and check the screens.
Newer Xcode versions can run an accessibility audit in UI tests. Check the current documentation for the exact call.

content.text: Apple renames and changes APIs and review rules often. The code and rules here come from our reading of the documentation and were not compiled or tested in Xcode, so check the current Apple documentation for your Xcode version before you rely on a detail.
Your task

items: Take one screen of your app and run the Accessibility Inspector audit. Fix every item it reports.
Switch to the largest accessibility text size. Find one layout that breaks and fix it with `@ScaledMetric` or `AnyLayout`.
Add an accessibility label to every icon-only button and test with VoiceOver on a real device.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Every icon-only button has a label.
No screen is broken at the largest text size.
Colour is never the only way to tell states apart.

steps.say: Standard SwiftUI controls already have much accessibility built in.
You add labels, values and traits where the default is not enough.
Using text styles and ScaledMetric keeps layouts working at large sizes.
You verify with the Accessibility Inspector and with VoiceOver on a real phone.

faqs.q: Do I need to add accessibility to every view?
faqs.a: No. Standard controls work already. Add labels to icon-only controls, group rows, mark headings, and check large text and contrast.

faqs.q: What is the quickest test?
faqs.a: Turn on VoiceOver on a real iPhone and try to finish a task with the screen curtain on. You will find the gaps in minutes.

faqs.q: Does accessibility matter for the App Store?
faqs.a: Apple encourages it and shows accessibility features in the listing. Some organisations and countries also require it, and it improves the experience for everyone.

quiz.q: What does an accessibilityLabel give an icon-only button?
How do you make text scale with the user's setting?
Why not rely on colour alone?
options: Some people cannot tell colours apart

lessons.title: iOS Localization: String Catalogs, Plurals, Formatting and Right-to-Left
lessons.description: Translate an iOS app with String Catalogs, plurals, number, date and currency formats, right-to-left layouts and pseudolanguages, and test each language.

content.text: An app in English reaches only part of the world. India alone has many languages, and a Hindi, Tamil or Marathi version can reach people your competitors ignore. **Localization** means preparing the app so that text, numbers, dates, currencies and layout all adapt to the user's language and region. **Internationalisation**, the step before it, means writing the code so that nothing is fixed to one language.

The most common mistake is to write text straight into the code and join pieces with `+`. That makes a translator's job impossible, because word order differs between languages. The fix is to keep every user-visible sentence whole, give it a key, and keep the translations in a catalog.
String Catalogs

Since Xcode 15, the recommended file is a **String Catalog**, with the extension `.xcstrings`. You add one to the project, add the languages in the project settings, and Xcode collects the strings it finds in your code. Each string shows its translations and a state such as "New", "Needs review" or "Translated", so you can see what is missing. A SwiftUI `Text("Welcome")` is localised automatically, because the text is treated as a key. For code that is not a view, use `String(localized:)`.

The `comment` argument is a note for the translator. A word such as "Save" can be a verb on a button or a noun in a game, and the translator cannot know which unless you say. Good comments are the cheapest quality improvement in localization.
Plurals

English has two plural forms, one and other. Some languages have more: Arabic has six, and Russian and Polish have several. In a String Catalog you right-click a string and choose **Vary by Plural**. Xcode then lets you type one translation for each form the language needs. Never write code such as `count == 1 ? "item" : "items"`, because it is correct only for English.
Numbers, dates and currency

Do not format these by hand. Use the formatters that follow the user's settings, so a number such as 1,234,567.89 appears as 12,34,567.89 for an Indian user and as 1.234.567,89 for a German user. Dates change order and month names too.

The currency code says which currency the amount is in. The locale decides how it is written. Mixing the two up is a common bug: a price in dollars is still dollars when a user in India looks at it, but it is written the way an Indian reader expects.
Right-to-left languages

Arabic, Hebrew and Urdu are written from right to left. SwiftUI flips the layout for you when you use `leading` and `trailing` instead of `left` and `right`. Use `.padding(.leading)` and `HStack`, not fixed left and right values. Images with a direction, such as an arrow that means "next", may need `.flipsForRightToLeftLayoutDirection(true)`. Check your screens with the right-to-left pseudolanguage in the scheme options.
Testing languages

items: In Xcode, edit the scheme, open Run > Options and set **App Language** to another language, or to a pseudolanguage such as Double-Length Pseudolanguage and Right-to-Left Pseudolanguage.
Double-length text shows where translated text overflows. It is the quickest way to find truncation.
Preview several languages with `.environment(\.locale, Locale(identifier: "ar"))` in your previews.
Ask a native speaker to review the translations in context. Machine translation is a starting point, not the finish.
Localize your App Store listing too: the name, subtitle, description and screenshots can all differ by language.

content.text: Apple renames and changes APIs and review rules often. The code and rules here come from our reading of the documentation and were not compiled or tested in Xcode, so check the current Apple documentation for your Xcode version before you rely on a detail.
Your task

items: Create a String Catalog, add Hindi, and translate five screens of strings.
Replace one hand-made plural with a catalog plural.
Run the app with the double-length and right-to-left pseudolanguages and fix what breaks.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: No user-visible sentence is built by joining pieces.
Dates, numbers and currencies use formatters.
Layouts use leading and trailing, and survive double-length text.

steps.say: The app uses whole sentences as keys, with placeholders for values.
The String Catalog holds a translation per language, including plural forms.
System formatters write numbers, dates and money the way the user expects.
The text, formats and layout direction all follow the user's language and region.

faqs.q: What is the difference between localization and internationalisation?
faqs.a: Internationalisation prepares the code so nothing is tied to one language. Localization adds the actual translations and regional formats.

faqs.q: Why not join strings with +?
faqs.a: Word order differs between languages, so a translator needs the whole sentence with placeholders to translate it correctly.

faqs.q: Should I use machine translation?
faqs.a: It is a useful first draft, but have a native speaker review it, especially for buttons, legal text and anything sensitive.

quiz.q: What file type is a String Catalog?
Why not join sentence pieces with +?
What should layouts use for right-to-left support?

lessons.title: iOS Widgets and App Intents: WidgetKit, Timelines, Siri and Shortcuts
lessons.metaTitle: iOS Widgets and App Intents with WidgetKit
lessons.description: Add a Home Screen widget with WidgetKit timelines and an App Group, and expose actions to Siri, Shortcuts and interactive widgets with App Intents.

content.text: A widget puts a small piece of your app on the Home Screen, the Lock Screen or the Today view. A habit app can show today's streak, a weather app the temperature, a shop app the order status. Widgets bring users back to the app, and they are a common feature in apps that feel well made.

A widget is **not a small running app**. It is a snapshot. The system asks your widget for a *timeline*, a list of entries with dates, and shows each entry at its time. Your widget cannot run code continuously, so you plan ahead: you hand the system everything it needs to draw the next hours.
The parts of a widget

items: **A widget extension**: a separate target you add with File > New > Target > Widget Extension.
**A TimelineEntry**: a struct with a `date` and the data to show.

**A TimelineProvider**: answers three questions. `placeholder` is a generic look while loading, `getSnapshot` is the preview in the widget gallery, and `getTimeline` returns the entries and when to ask again.
**A view**: SwiftUI, with the same views and modifiers you already know.
**An App Group**: a shared container so the app and widget can read the same data.

content.text: The group name `group.com.example.habits` is an example. You create the real one in Signing & Capabilities by adding the App Groups capability to **both** the app and the widget extension. When the app changes the data, it saves it into the shared container and calls `WidgetCenter.shared.reloadAllTimelines()` so the widget refreshes sooner than its normal schedule.
Refresh limits

The system gives each widget a limited budget of refreshes per day, so you cannot update every second. Use a timeline with several entries when you know the future, such as a countdown or a schedule, and use `reloadTimelines` only when the data really changed. A widget that tries to show live data constantly will simply show stale data, and users will think it is broken.
App Intents: actions for Siri, Shortcuts and widgets

An **App Intent** describes something your app can do, in a form the system understands. Once you define one, it can appear in the Shortcuts app, be spoken to Siri, appear in Spotlight and, since iOS 17, run from a button in a widget without opening the app. The code is a struct with a title, optional parameters and a `perform` function.

`HabitStorage` is the same storage object your app uses. This is the key design rule: put the real work in a shared function or package, and let the screen, the widget and the intent all call it. If each has its own copy of the logic, they will drift apart.

Design widgets for a glance. People look at a widget for about a second, so show one number, one status or one next action, not a miniature of the whole app. Support the sizes that make sense, test in light and dark mode, and give the widget a tap target that opens the right screen in the app with `widgetURL`. A widget that opens the app on the home screen instead of the relevant detail feels careless.

Widgets must also respect privacy. They can appear on the Lock Screen, where other people can see them. Do not show private details such as a message text or a balance there unless the user chooses to. The `redacted` and `privacySensitive` modifiers let you hide content when the device is locked.

Apple renames and changes APIs and review rules often. The code and rules here come from our reading of the documentation and were not compiled or tested in Xcode, so check the current Apple documentation for your Xcode version before you rely on a detail.
Your task

items: Add a widget extension to the Habit tracker project and show the best streak.
Create an App Group, share the streak value and reload the widget when a habit is ticked.
Add an App Intent and run it from the Shortcuts app.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The widget shows real data from the app.
The widget refreshes after a change in the app.
The intent and the screen use the same function.

animation.title: App, widget and intent share data

steps.say: The app saves a value and asks widgets to reload.
The value lives in an App Group container that both targets can read.
The widget provider reads it and returns a timeline of entries.
The system draws the entries on the Home Screen, and App Intents run from Siri and Shortcuts.

faqs.q: Can a widget run code all the time?
faqs.a: No. It shows entries from a timeline that you provide, and refreshes are limited by the system. Plan the timeline ahead.

faqs.q: Why do I need an App Group?
faqs.a: The app and the widget are separate processes and cannot see each other's files. An App Group gives them a shared container.

faqs.q: What are App Intents used for?
faqs.a: They describe actions that Siri, Shortcuts, Spotlight and interactive widgets can run. They make your app useful outside its own screens.

quiz.q: What does a widget show?
options: Entries from a timeline you provide

quiz.q: Why does a widget need an App Group?
options: The app and widget are separate processes

quiz.q: What does an App Intent describe?
options: An action Siri, Shortcuts and widgets can run

lessons.title: App Store Privacy and Review: Privacy Manifests, Guidelines and Common Rejections
lessons.metaTitle: App Store Privacy and Review Guidelines
lessons.description: Prepare an iOS app for App Store review: privacy manifests, privacy labels, permission texts, account deletion, purchase rules and common rejections.

content.text: Apps are reviewed by people and by automated checks before they appear in the App Store. A rejection usually costs one to a few days, and some rejections come from the same small mistakes again and again. This lesson lists what reviewers look for, so you can fix it before you submit. It also covers **privacy**, which Apple treats as a core promise to its users and checks more closely every year.

Apple changes its App Store Review Guidelines, privacy requirements and deadlines regularly. This lesson is a checklist built from our reading of the guidelines and was not tested against a real submission. Before you submit, read the current App Store Review Guidelines and the current App Store Connect help pages.
Privacy information you must provide

items: **App Privacy details (privacy labels)**: in App Store Connect you list what data the app and its libraries collect, whether it is linked to the user, and whether it is used for tracking. These appear on your listing. They must be accurate, including data collected by third-party SDKs such as analytics and ads.

**Privacy policy URL**: a public page that says what you collect and why, how users can ask for deletion, and how to contact you. Apps need one, and apps that handle account or health data must be especially clear.

**Privacy manifest (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy)**: a file in your app, and in the SDKs you include, that declares the data types collected and the reasons for using certain system APIs. Apple has required manifests for specific commonly used SDKs and for apps that use specific APIs. Check which of your dependencies provide one.

**Required reason APIs**: some system APIs, such as file timestamps, system boot time, disk space and UserDefaults, can be used to fingerprint a device. When your app or a library uses them, you must declare an approved reason in the manifest.

**App Tracking Transparency**: if you track users across other companies' apps and sites, you must ask with the ATT prompt and explain why. If you do not track, do not show the prompt, and do not claim tracking in the label.

content.text: Permission texts

Every sensitive permission needs a **usage description** in Info.plist, such as `NSCameraUsageDescription` or `NSHealthShareUsageDescription`. The text must say in plain words why your app needs it. "We need the camera" is weak. "The camera scans QR codes. Pictures are not saved or sent anywhere" is strong. Missing or vague texts cause rejections, and a missing key crashes the app when it asks. Ask for a permission only at the moment the feature needs it, after explaining it on your own screen.
Rules that surprise first-time submitters

items: **Account deletion**: if users can create an account inside the app, they must also be able to start deleting that account inside the app. A link to a website form alone is not enough under the guidelines at the time of writing.

**Sign in with Apple**: apps that offer other third-party social logins have been required to offer an equivalent privacy-focused option such as Sign in with Apple. The exact rule has changed over time, so read the current guideline.

**In-app purchase**: digital goods and features inside the app, such as premium content or subscriptions, generally must use Apple's In-App Purchase. Physical goods and services consumed outside the app, such as a taxi ride, do not. There are specific exceptions and regional rules, so read section 3.1 of the guidelines.
**Demo account**: if the app needs a login, give the reviewer a working demo account in App Store Connect, with sample data. A reviewer who cannot get in will reject the app.
**Completeness**: no placeholder text, empty screens, broken links or "coming soon" features. The reviewer opens every tab.
**Accurate metadata**: screenshots must show the real app. Do not mention other platforms or use another company's trademarks in the name.
**Minimum functionality**: an app that only wraps a website, or is a thin copy of another app, is at risk of rejection under the design guidelines.
**User-generated content**: if users can post, you need filtering, a way to report content, a way to block abusive users and a way to contact you.
**AI features**: be clear when content is generated by AI, and follow the rules for user-generated content and for sending personal data to third parties.

content.text: A pre-submission checklist

items: Build the release configuration and test it on a real device, not only the Simulator. Some bugs appear only in release builds.
Check that every usage description exists and is specific.
Check the privacy manifest and that App Privacy answers match what the app and every SDK really do.
Test with no network, a slow network and a fresh install. The reviewer often starts from a clean device.
Open every screen and button. Remove or hide unfinished features.
Check Dynamic Type, Dark Mode and the smallest supported iPhone.
Fill in the review notes: how to log in, how to reach hidden features, and any hardware needed.
Use TestFlight for a final round with real testers before you submit.

content.text: If you are rejected

A rejection is a conversation. Read the message carefully: it quotes a guideline number. Fix exactly that issue, reply in Resolution Center if you need to explain something, and resubmit. If you believe the reviewer made a mistake, you can reply politely with evidence or request an appeal. Do not resubmit the same build without changes, and do not argue emotionally. Most rejections are resolved in one or two rounds.
Your task

items: Write a one-page privacy summary for an app you built: what it collects, why, where it is stored, and how a user deletes it.
List every third-party SDK and check whether it needs a privacy manifest.
Rewrite every usage description in your app so a stranger understands why it is needed.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your privacy labels match the app's real behaviour.
Every permission has a clear usage text.
A reviewer could sign in with your demo account and reach every feature.

steps.say: You build the release version and test it on a real device.
You prepare privacy labels, the manifest, permission texts and a demo account.
Reviewers open every screen and check the guidelines.
If approved the app goes live. If rejected, fix the quoted guideline and resubmit.

faqs.q: How long does App Review take?
faqs.a: It is often a day or two, but it varies. Plan extra time for a first submission, and do not schedule a launch for the same day.

faqs.q: Do I need a privacy policy if I collect nothing?
faqs.a: A policy URL is still required for the listing. Say plainly what you do and do not collect.

faqs.q: What is the most common reason for rejection?
faqs.a: Crashes and bugs, incomplete features, missing demo accounts and unclear permission or privacy information are among the most frequent. Testing the release build on a device prevents many of them.

quiz.q: What must every sensitive permission have?
options: A clear usage description in Info.plist

quiz.q: What should you give reviewers if the app needs a login?
What should you do after a rejection?
options: Fix the quoted guideline and resubmit

lessons.title: Core Data in Depth for iOS: Stacks, Contexts, Fetch Requests and Migration
lessons.metaTitle: Core Data in Depth: Contexts and Migration
lessons.description: Learn Core Data for older and larger iOS projects: the container, contexts, fetch requests, background saves, migration and when SwiftData is better.

content.text: SwiftData is the modern way to store data in an iOS app, but Core Data is still everywhere. It has been part of iOS for many years, and a large share of the apps you will work on in a job were built with it. You will read Core Data code in existing projects, and interviewers still ask about it. This lesson teaches the ideas you need to read it, fix it and decide when to migrate to SwiftData.

Core Data details change between iOS versions. The code below is from our reading of the documentation and was not compiled or tested here. Compare it with the current Apple documentation, and test migrations on copies of real data before shipping.
The four main objects

items: **NSManagedObjectModel**: describes your entities, their attributes and relationships. You usually design it visually in an `.xcdatamodeld` file in Xcode.
**NSPersistentStoreCoordinator**: connects the model to the actual store on disk, usually a SQLite database.
**NSManagedObjectContext**: a scratchpad. You fetch objects into a context, change them, and then save the context to write the changes. Contexts are **not thread-safe**.
**NSPersistentContainer**: bundles the three above into one object, so you rarely build them by hand.

content.text: `viewContext` is the context tied to the main thread, which your UI reads. The `inMemory` option is the Core Data version of the in-memory store trick from the To-Do project: tests use a store that disappears afterwards. In a real app, handle a load failure with a clear message instead of `fatalError`.
Create, fetch, update and delete

A **predicate** filters, and a **sort descriptor** orders. The `fetchBatchSize` tells Core Data to load objects in batches as you read them, which saves memory on large lists. In SwiftUI, the `@FetchRequest` property wrapper does the same job as SwiftData's `@Query`: it fetches and keeps the list updated.
Background work

Never do heavy work on the main context, because it freezes the screen. Use a **background context**. `container.performBackgroundTask` gives you a fresh context on its own queue. Objects from one context must never be used in another. Pass `NSManagedObjectID` values between contexts and fetch the object again in the other one.

In a modern codebase, a `@MainActor` repository class that owns `viewContext`, and a background context for imports, keeps the threading rules in one place. The Core Data multithreading debugging flag, `-com.apple.CoreData.ConcurrencyDebug 1`, in the scheme arguments, makes the app crash early when you touch a context from the wrong queue. That is much better than a rare, random crash in production.
Migration

When you change the model, old data must be converted. **Lightweight migration** handles simple changes automatically: adding an attribute with a default or optional value, renaming with a renaming identifier, or adding an entity. It is on by default for the persistent container when you create a new model version. More complex changes need a **mapping model** or custom code. The safe process is always the same: add a new model version, never edit an old one that shipped, test the upgrade from every older version you released, and keep a copy of real-looking data for those tests.
Core Data or SwiftData?

items: **New project, iOS 17 and later**: SwiftData is usually simpler and works naturally with SwiftUI.
**Existing Core Data app**: do not rewrite it only because SwiftData exists. Migrate when there is a clear benefit, in small steps, and test migration carefully.

**Older iOS versions or needs SwiftData does not yet cover**: Core Data is mature and fully documented. Check the current SwiftData documentation for gaps such as shared databases, complex migrations and CloudKit sharing.

content.text: Your task

items: Create a Core Data project with an entity, fetch it with `@FetchRequest` and add a delete action.
Write a test that uses an in-memory container and checks a fetch with a predicate.
Add the concurrency debug flag to your scheme and trigger the crash on purpose by using `viewContext` from a background task.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Contexts are only used on their own queue.
A background import does not freeze the UI.
Every shipped model version stays in the project for migration.

steps.say: The model describes entities, attributes and relationships.
NSPersistentContainer builds the coordinator and loads the store.
You work in contexts: the view context for the UI, background contexts for heavy work.
Saving a context writes the changes to the SQLite store.

faqs.q: Is Core Data a database?
faqs.a: It is an object graph and persistence framework. It usually stores data in SQLite, but you work with objects, not SQL.

faqs.q: Why must I not share objects between contexts?
faqs.a: Contexts are not thread-safe. Pass the object ID and fetch it again in the other context.

faqs.q: Should I migrate to SwiftData now?
faqs.a: Only when there is a clear benefit. For a working app, a careful gradual move is safer than a full rewrite.

quiz.q: Are managed object contexts thread-safe?
options: No, use each on its own queue

quiz.q: What is a lightweight migration?
options: Automatic conversion for simple model changes

quiz.q: How do you move an object between contexts?
options: Pass its object ID and fetch it again

lessons.title: Modular iOS Architecture: Swift Packages, Clean Architecture and Performance
lessons.metaTitle: Modular iOS Apps: SPM, Clean Architecture
lessons.description: Split a growing app into Swift packages, apply Clean Architecture layers, wire dependencies at one composition root, and profile launch, memory and scrolling.

content.text: A small app can live in one target. A big one cannot, for three reasons: builds get slow, any file can depend on any other so changes ripple everywhere, and several people cannot work in parallel without conflicts. **Modularisation** and a clear **architecture** are the answer, and *how would you structure a large app?* is a standard senior question. This lesson shows the practical version: Swift packages, layers, one place that wires everything, and the tools that find performance problems.
Swift Package Manager for your own code

Swift Package Manager (SPM) is built into Xcode. It adds third-party libraries, and it also lets you split *your own* code into **local packages**, each with its own tests. A package describes its targets in a `Package.swift` file.

items: Add it to the app with **File > Add Package Dependencies > Add Local**, then link the library to the app target.

Anything another module must see has to be marked **`public`**, including `init`s. The default access level, `internal`, hides things outside their own module. This is both the pain and the point of modules: they force you to decide what each one offers.

Dependencies must point one way. In the package above, `ExpensesData` knows `ExpensesDomain`, and `ExpensesDomain` knows nothing about `ExpensesData`. If you try to make a circle, the build fails, and that is useful.

content.text: Clean Architecture in three layers
Clean Architecture says that *business rules must not depend on details*. For an iOS app that becomes three layers, with the arrows pointing inward.

items: **Domain:** your entities (`Expense`), the rules, **use cases** (`AddExpense`), and **protocols** for what the outside must provide (`ExpenseRepository`). Pure Swift, with no SwiftUI, no SwiftData, no networking. It is the easiest layer to test.
**Data:** the real work behind those protocols: a SwiftData store, a REST client, a cache. It imports Domain.
**Presentation:** SwiftUI views and view models. It asks use cases for things and turns them into screen state.

content.text: The rule *a title cannot be empty and the amount must be above zero* now lives in one place, with no screen. It is tested with a fake repository in a few lines, and it works the same if you move from SwiftData to a server next year. A view model calls `try await addExpense(title: t, amount: a)`, and nothing else changes.
The composition root: where everything is wired

Someone has to create the real objects and hand them in. Do it **in one place**, near the start of the app, called the *composition root*. Everywhere else just receives what it needs, the dependency injection from the first course, now at app scale.

`SwiftDataExpenseRepository` and `InMemoryExpenseRepository` are your own types in the Data module, which implement `ExpenseRepository`. Real ones need a model container, and the details are in the SwiftData lessons.
Frameworks you will hear about

items: **The Composable Architecture (TCA)** is a popular third-party library, from Point-Free, for state management with strict, testable rules. It is powerful and has a real learning curve. A team should adopt it together, not one person alone.

**Dependency containers** such as *Factory* or *Swinject*: libraries that register and resolve dependencies. Many teams find that plain initialiser injection and a small environment struct, as above, are enough.
**Third-party packages in general:** pin versions, read the licence, and ask whether the library will still be maintained in two years. Each package is code you now own.

content.text: When not to modularise

Every module is extra set-up and extra `public` keywords. For one developer and a few screens, a single target with clear folders is better. Split when builds become slow, when teams collide, or when a part such as the design system or the network layer is reused by more than one app. Architecture should answer a problem you have, and not one you imagine.
Performance: measure first
Feelings about speed are often wrong. Use Xcode's tools.

items: **Time Profiler** (Instruments) shows which functions use the CPU. Look at the *heaviest stack trace*. The slow part is often not the one you suspect.
**Allocations and Leaks** show memory growth, as in lesson 3.
**Hangs** and the **SwiftUI** template in Instruments show moments when the main thread was blocked, and how often a view body ran.
**App launch** time matters. Do as little as possible before the first screen: no network calls, no big file reads, no setting up of every service. Start the rest after the first frame.

**Images** are the usual cause of memory spikes. A 12-megapixel photo shown in a 100-point thumbnail should be **downsampled**, for example with `UIImage.preparingThumbnail(of:)`, and not decoded at full size.
**Lists:** use lazy containers, stable ids and cheap row views. Avoid `AnyView`, which hides the real type from SwiftUI and can make updates slower.
**Field data:** Xcode's Organizer shows crash and hang reports from real users, and `MetricKit` delivers performance numbers from the field. Your own phone on fast Wi-Fi is not your users.

content.text: `measure` runs the block several times and reports the average. Xcode lets you save a *baseline*, so a later change that makes the code much slower fails the test.
Common mistakes

items: Splitting into twenty modules on day one.
A Domain module that imports SwiftUI or SwiftData, which breaks the idea.
Optimising before measuring.
Putting every service in a global singleton. It hides dependencies and makes tests hard.

content.text: Your task

items: Move your Expense model, a repository protocol and one use case into a local Swift package called `ExpensesKit`, with its own tests.
Add an in-memory repository and use it in a `#Preview` through an `AppEnvironment`.
Run the Time Profiler on your app's launch and write down the three heaviest calls.
Show a large image in a thumbnail, then downsample it and compare memory in the debug navigator.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The Domain package builds and tests with no import of SwiftUI or SwiftData.
Previews work with fake data and no network.
You can describe the three layers and which way their dependencies point.

steps.say: Presentation shows state and asks the Domain layer to do things.
Domain holds the rules and knows nothing about screens or databases.
It states what it needs as a protocol, such as a repository.
The Data layer implements the protocol, so you can swap a database for a server without touching the rules.

faqs.q: Why split an iOS app into Swift packages?
faqs.a: To speed up builds, to stop any file depending on any other, to let teams work in parallel, and to reuse parts such as a design system. For a small app with one developer, one target is usually better.

faqs.q: What is a composition root?
faqs.a: The one place near the start of the app where real objects are created and handed to the parts that need them. The rest of the code only receives dependencies.

faqs.q: How do I find out why my app is slow?
faqs.a: Measure with Instruments, for example Time Profiler for CPU, Allocations for memory and the Hangs and SwiftUI templates for the main thread. Do not guess, and check field data in Xcode Organizer and MetricKit.

quiz.q: In Clean Architecture, which layer should not import SwiftUI or SwiftData?
What is a composition root?
options: The one place where real objects are created and injected

quiz.q: What should you do before optimising performance?

notes: Local Swift packages split an app: faster builds, clear dependencies, parallel work. Mark shared things `public`.
Layers point inward: Presentation, Domain (rules, use cases, protocols), Data (implementations).
Domain imports no SwiftUI or SwiftData, so it is easy to test.
Composition root: one place creates real objects and injects them (`AppEnvironment.live()` and `.preview()`).
Do not modularise a small app on day one. Split when a real problem appears.
Measure first: Time Profiler, Allocations, Hangs. Keep launch light, downsample images, avoid AnyView.

lessons.title: iOS CI/CD: Fastlane, GitHub Actions, Xcode Cloud and Safe Releases
lessons.metaTitle: iOS CI/CD: Fastlane, Actions, Xcode Cloud
lessons.description: Automate iOS builds and tests, ship to TestFlight with Fastlane, compare GitHub Actions, Xcode Cloud and Bitrise, and release safely with flags.

content.text: Releasing an iOS app by hand means a dozen careful clicks: bump the number, archive, sign, upload, wait, fill in a form. Each click is a chance to forget something, and the person who knows the steps goes on holiday. **Continuous integration** (CI) builds and tests the app on a server for every change, and **continuous delivery** (CD) ships it with little or no hand work. Knowing this separates a developer who writes screens from one who can own a release.
What CI should do on every change

items: Check out the code on a clean machine.
Resolve packages.
Build the app.
Run the unit tests, and the UI tests for the main flows.
Report the result on the pull request, so a broken change cannot be merged by mistake.

content.text: Because the machine starts clean, CI also finds the classic *works on my machine* problems, such as a file that is on your computer but was never committed.
Command line first
Every CI tool does the same underlying thing: it runs `xcodebuild`. If you can run these in a terminal, you can automate them.

xcodebuild test \
  -scheme ExpenseTracker \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 16' \
  -resultBundlePath build/TestResults.xcresult

Simulator names and the Xcode version differ between machines and CI images. If the run fails with a message about a missing destination, run `xcrun simctl list devices` on the same machine to see what exists, and use one of those names.
GitHub Actions

If your code is on GitHub, Actions is the easiest place to start. A workflow is a YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. iOS builds need a **macOS runner**, which GitHub bills at a higher rate than Linux. Check the current pricing and your free allowance.

name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: macos-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Show Xcode version
        run: xcodebuild -version
      - name: Test
        run: |
          xcodebuild test \
            -scheme ExpenseTracker \
            -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 16'

items: Pin the Xcode version your project needs if the runner has several, and check the runner image's documentation for how to select it.
Cache Swift package downloads to save minutes.
Keep secrets, such as keys, in **GitHub Secrets** and never in the repository.

content.text: Fastlane: scripts for releases

**Fastlane** is a toolbox of release actions written in Ruby, with a simple file called a `Fastfile`. A *lane* is a named sequence of steps. Teams use it so that *ship a beta* is one command that works the same on every machine.

default_platform(:ios)

platform :ios do
  desc "Run the unit tests"
  lane :test do
    run_tests(scheme: "ExpenseTracker", devices: ["iPhone 16"])
  end

  desc "Build and upload to TestFlight"
  lane :beta do
    api_key = app_store_connect_api_key(
      key_id: ENV["ASC_KEY_ID"],
      issuer_id: ENV["ASC_ISSUER_ID"],
      key_content: ENV["ASC_KEY_CONTENT"]
    )
    increment_build_number(build_number: latest_testflight_build_number(api_key: api_key) + 1)
    build_app(scheme: "ExpenseTracker")
    upload_to_testflight(api_key: api_key)
  end
end

items: `run_tests`, `build_app` and `upload_to_testflight` are the current names for the older `scan`, `gym` and `pilot` actions, and the old names still work. Check Fastlane's documentation for your version.
The **App Store Connect API key** lets automation sign in without your personal password. Create it in App Store Connect, give it the least role it needs, and store its contents in your CI's secrets.

**Code signing** is the part that hurts most. The simplest route is Xcode's automatic signing. For teams, `fastlane match` keeps the certificates and profiles in a private repository, so every machine uses the same ones.

content.text: Xcode Cloud and other services

items: **Xcode Cloud** is Apple's own CI/CD, set up inside Xcode and App Store Connect. It handles signing for you and sends builds to TestFlight. Check Apple's pages for the current plans and free allowance.
**Bitrise** and similar services are hosted for mobile and give ready-made steps and a visual editor.
**Self-hosted Mac machines** are an option for teams with many builds. Someone has to keep them updated.

content.text: The choice usually depends on where the code lives, the budget and how much control the team wants. All of them run the same `xcodebuild` underneath, so what you learn here transfers.
Versions and build numbers

items: The **version** (for example 2.4.0) is what people see. It follows a pattern the team agrees on, such as *major.minor.patch*.
The **build number** must go up with every upload to App Store Connect. Automate it, as in the lane above, so nobody has to remember.

content.text: Releasing without fear

items: **TestFlight first.** Every release goes to testers before the public.
**Phased release.** App Store Connect can release an update to a growing share of automatic-update users over several days. If crash reports rise, you can pause it.

**Feature flags** hide new code behind a switch that you control from a server or a config file. You can ship code that is turned off, turn it on for a few people, and turn it off again without a new release. Keep the flag list small and delete old flags.
**Crash reporting.** Xcode Organizer shows crashes from users. Third-party tools such as Firebase Crashlytics or Sentry add more detail and alerts.
**A hotfix path.** Decide in advance how you ship a fix quickly: a branch from the release tag, a short review, the same pipeline. Practice it once when nothing is on fire.
**Release notes** that say what changed, in plain words.

content.text: An App Store review can take time, so a fix is never instant. This is why flags, phased release and server-side control of risky behaviour matter more on iOS than on the web.
Common mistakes

items: Committing keys or certificates to the repository.
A CI that is red for weeks, so everyone ignores it. Fix or remove failing tests quickly.
Manual build numbers that clash.
Shipping to everyone at once with no way to pause.

content.text: Your task

items: Write the GitHub Actions workflow and open a pull request that runs it. Break a test on purpose and watch the check fail.
Write the `test` lane in a `Fastfile` and run it with `fastlane test`.
Create an App Store Connect API key (only if you have a developer account), store it as secrets and write the `beta` lane.
Write a one-page release checklist for your app, including the hotfix steps.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A failing test blocks the pull request.
`fastlane test` runs the same tests as CI.
You can explain phased release and a feature flag, and when each helps.

steps.say: A developer opens a pull request with a change.
CI builds the app on a clean machine and runs the tests. A failure blocks the merge.
After merge, a lane increments the build number and sends the build to TestFlight.
The release goes to users in phases. If crashes rise, you can pause it.

faqs.q: What is the difference between CI and CD?
faqs.a: CI (continuous integration) builds and tests every change automatically. CD (continuous delivery) goes further and packages and ships the app, for example to TestFlight, with little or no manual work.

faqs.q: Is Fastlane still used?
faqs.a: Yes, many teams use it to script builds, signing, screenshots and uploads, often inside CI services. Xcode Cloud and other tools cover some of the same ground, and all of them run xcodebuild underneath.

faqs.q: How do I release safely on iOS where review takes time?
faqs.a: Use TestFlight first, phased release, feature flags you can switch from a server, crash reporting, and a hotfix path you have already practised.

quiz.q: What should CI do on every pull request?
options: Build the app and run the tests on a clean machine

quiz.q: What is a feature flag?
options: A switch that turns code on or off without a new release

quiz.q: Where should signing keys and API keys be kept in CI?
options: In the CI secrets, never in the repository

notes: CI: clean checkout, build, test, report on the pull request. Underneath it is `xcodebuild test`.
GitHub Actions needs a macOS runner (check pricing). Keep keys in Secrets.
Fastlane lanes: `run_tests`, `build_app`, `upload_to_testflight`. Use an App Store Connect API key.
Signing is the hard part: automatic signing, or `fastlane match` for teams.
Xcode Cloud (Apple), Bitrise, self-hosted Macs: all run xcodebuild.
Release safely: TestFlight, phased release, feature flags, crash reporting, a practised hotfix path.

lessons.title: Senior iOS Interview Preparation: Questions, System Design and Portfolio
lessons.description: Prepare for iOS interviews beyond the basics: Swift, concurrency, SwiftUI and architecture questions, a mobile system design walkthrough and your portfolio.

content.text: By now you know the topics. An interview asks something different: *can you explain it, choose between options and defend the choice?* This lesson gives you a way to prepare. We cannot know what any one company will ask, and we do not claim that these questions were asked anywhere in particular. They are common, current topics, and the best answers are your **own words, with an example from your own project**.
How interviews usually go

items: **A screen of your resume and portfolio.** Be ready to explain every project in a minute.
**Language and framework questions**, short answers, to check your base.
**Live coding or a take-home task.** A small feature, often a list with a network call and a detail screen.
**Architecture or system design**: how you would build a larger feature or app.
**Talking about work with others:** disagreements, mistakes, reviews.

content.text: Swift questions, with the ideas behind the answers

items: **Struct or class?** Value versus reference semantics, copying, identity, inheritance, and why SwiftUI uses structs. Give an example of a bug caused by shared reference.
**What is ARC? What is a retain cycle?** Strong references and counts, weak versus unowned, `[weak self]`, and how you find a leak (Memory Graph, Instruments).
**What is an optional?** The type that can hold nothing, safe unwrapping, and why force unwrapping is risky.
**Protocols versus inheritance?** Composition, protocol extensions, multiple conformance, testing with fakes.
**What does `escaping` mean for a closure?** The closure may be called after the function returns, so it is stored, and may capture `self`.
**Generics and `some` versus `any`?** One type known at compile time versus a box that holds any type.

content.text: Concurrency questions

items: **GCD and OperationQueue versus async/await?** Callbacks and queues versus structured code that reads in order, with cancellation and error handling built in.
**What is an actor?** Isolated state that handles one call at a time. Mention reentrancy.
**What does `@MainActor` do?** Runs code on the main thread, so UI updates are safe.
**How do you cancel a search as the user types?** Keep the task, cancel it on each change, add a short delay, check `Task.isCancelled`.
**What is a data race, and how does Swift help?** Two threads using the same data with one writing. `Sendable`, actors and strict concurrency checks.

content.text: SwiftUI questions

items: **`@State`, `@Binding`, `@Observable`, `@Environment`: when each?** Own local value, share a value with a child, an observable model object, a value or object from the environment.
**Why did my view update, or not update?** Which state it reads, identity, and what a view body is allowed to do.
**`ObservableObject` versus `@Observable`?** The older `@Published` approach versus the iOS 17 macro that tracks the properties a view reads.
**How do you navigate from code?** `NavigationStack` with a `NavigationPath` and a router.
**How do you mix SwiftUI and UIKit?** `UIHostingController` and `UIViewRepresentable`.

content.text: Architecture and platform questions

items: **MVC, MVVM, Clean Architecture, TCA: how do you choose?** Team size, testing needs, the size of the app, and the cost of each. Say what you would do on a small app and on a large one.
**How do you handle auth tokens?** Keychain, refresh through one shared task, never log them.
**How do you test a view model?** Inject a fake service through a protocol, call the method, check the state.
**How do you make an app work offline?** A local database as the source of truth, a sync step, clear states for *offline* and *stale*.
**How do you speed up a slow list or a slow launch?** Measure with Instruments first, then fix the biggest cause.

content.text: A system design walkthrough: an offline-first expense app that syncs

Interviewers like a design question because there is no single right answer. They watch how you *think*. Here is a way to organise the answer, using our own app. Talk through it out loud, and ask questions before you start.

items: **Clarify.** Who uses it? Do they need it offline? How many records? Several devices per person? Any shared accounts?
**Local first.** The device database (SwiftData or Core Data) is the **source of truth** for the screen. The screen never waits for the network.

**A sync layer.** Changes made offline go into a queue of pending operations (create, update, delete), each with a client-generated id and a timestamp. When the network is back, a worker sends them in order, with retries and backoff, and marks each one done.
**Conflicts.** Two devices edit the same item. Say your rule: *last write wins* is simple, and field-level merging is safer. Tell them what you trade away.
**Server API.** Incremental pull with a *since* cursor, so the app asks only for changes. Pagination for large lists. Idempotent writes, so a retry cannot create duplicates.
**Auth and security.** Tokens in the Keychain, refresh handled once, HTTPS, no secrets in the app.
**Push.** A silent push tells the app that something changed, and the app pulls. Remember that delivery is not guaranteed.
**Errors and states.** Loading, empty, offline, failed with retry, syncing. Say what the user sees in each.
**Testing and rollout.** Unit tests for the sync rules with fake services, a feature flag, a phased release, crash reporting.

content.text: A good answer names the *trade-offs*, not only the parts. For example: *local-first makes the app feel fast and work offline, but adds sync and conflict logic, which is where most of the bugs will be.*
Live coding and take-home tips

items: Read the brief twice. Ask what is in scope and what is not.
Get a small working version first, and improve it. A running app beats a perfect plan.
Keep the structure simple, with a view model and a protocol for the network, and show you can test it.
Handle loading, empty and error states. Many people forget them.
Write a short README: how to run it, what you chose, and what you would do next.

content.text: Your portfolio

items: Three to four **finished** projects are better than ten half-done ones. Link the code, add screenshots and, if you can, a TestFlight or App Store link.
In each README, explain **one hard decision** and why you made it. This is what interviewers talk about.
Show tests, a clean structure and a continuous integration badge.
Keep your resume honest and specific. List the frameworks you really used, and what you built with them.

content.text: Build your resume with our [resume builder](/app) and check it with the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker). Practise on the [interview questions page](/jobs/interview-questions), and read the [roadmaps](/roadmaps) to plan what to add next. If you have not done it yet, the [beginner iOS course](/learn/ios-development-swift-swiftui-course) and our [Git and GitHub course](/learn/git-and-github-course) cover the base that these questions assume.
No preparation can promise an offer, because hiring depends on many things you do not control. What you can control is being able to explain, with examples, what you built and why.
Your task

items: Pick ten questions from this lesson and answer each aloud in under a minute. Record yourself and listen back.
Write a one-page system design for an app of your choice, using the nine steps above.
Choose your best project and write the README with one hard decision and its trade-offs.
Ask a friend to ask you three questions you did not prepare, and practise saying *I am not sure, but here is how I would find out*.

items: You can explain value versus reference types, ARC and actors in your own words, with one example each.
Your system design names at least two trade-offs.
Your best project has a README that a stranger could follow.

steps.say: The screen always reads from the local database, so it is fast and works offline.
User changes are saved locally at once and added to a queue of pending operations.
When the network is back, a worker sends the queue to the server, with retries and idempotent writes.
The server answers with changes since a cursor, and the app merges them using your conflict rule.

faqs.q: What is asked in a senior iOS interview?
faqs.a: It varies by company, so we cannot say what any one will ask. Expect Swift and concurrency fundamentals, SwiftUI and UIKit, architecture choices, testing, performance and a design discussion, and be ready to explain your own projects.

faqs.q: How should I answer a system design question?
faqs.a: Clarify the requirements first, then walk through the data flow, offline behaviour, sync and conflicts, security, errors and testing. Name the trade-offs of your choices instead of only listing parts.

faqs.q: How many portfolio projects do I need?
faqs.a: Three or four finished and well explained projects are stronger than many unfinished ones. A README that explains one hard decision helps a lot.

What makes a system design answer strong?

Listing as many tools as possible

lessons.title: iOS Interview Questions and Answers: Swift, SwiftUI, Concurrency and Architecture
lessons.description: Practise iOS interview questions with short model answers on Swift, memory, concurrency, SwiftUI, architecture, data, security, testing and release.

content.text: This lesson is a question bank for iOS interviews, from junior to senior level. Each answer is short on purpose, so you can learn the idea and then say it in your own words. In a real interview, an answer that is clear and honest beats a memorised one. If you do not know something, say what you do know and how you would find out. Good interviewers care more about how you think than about whether you recall every name.

The answers are written from our reading of Swift and Apple's documentation and may be out of date for the newest Xcode and iOS versions. We list a starter set, not the only questions you may be asked. Verify details that matter before you repeat them, and practise by building the projects in this and the beginner course.
How to answer well

items: **Define the idea in one sentence.** For example, "ARC frees an object when nothing strongly refers to it."
**Give a small example.** A short piece of code or a real situation from your project shows you have used it.
**Name a trade-off or a pitfall.** This is what separates a junior from a senior answer.
**Stop.** Do not keep talking after the answer is complete. Let the interviewer ask more.

content.text: Swift language

items: **What is the difference between a struct and a class?** A struct is a value type and is copied on assignment. A class is a reference type and is shared. Structs have no inheritance. Prefer structs for simple data and use classes when you need shared identity or inheritance.
**What does copy-on-write mean?** Collections such as Array share their storage until one copy is changed. Only then is the storage actually copied, so copying an array is cheap until you mutate it.
**What is an optional?** An enum with two cases, some value or none (nil). It makes missing values explicit, and the compiler forces you to handle them.

**What is the difference between if let and guard let?** `if let` unwraps for use inside its own block. `guard let` unwraps for use in the rest of the scope and must exit if the value is nil. Guard keeps the main path unindented.

**What does force unwrapping do and when is it acceptable?** `!` crashes if the value is nil. It is acceptable only when nil would be a programmer error, for example an outlet that must exist. Prefer safe unwrapping.

**What is a protocol? What is protocol-oriented programming?** A protocol lists requirements that types can adopt. Protocol-oriented programming favours composing behaviour with protocols and extensions, instead of deep class hierarchies.

**What is the difference between a protocol with associated types and a plain protocol?** Associated types make a protocol generic over some type, such as the element type of a collection. A protocol with them cannot be used as a plain type in the same way, and you use generics or `some` and `any`.

**What is the difference between `some` and `any`?** `some Protocol` means one specific hidden type, chosen by the implementation, so the compiler knows it. `any Protocol` is an existential box that can hold different types at run time, with some cost.
**What are generics and why use them?** They let you write one function or type that works with many types while staying type-safe, for example a `Stack<Element>`.

**What is a closure, and what does it capture?** A function that can be passed around. It captures the variables it uses from the surrounding scope, which can create retain cycles if it captures `self` strongly.

**What is the difference between @escaping and non-escaping closures?** A non-escaping closure runs before the function returns. An escaping closure can be stored and called later, so the compiler is stricter about capturing `self`.

**What is the difference between map, flatMap, compactMap and filter?** `map` transforms each item. `compactMap` transforms and drops nils. `flatMap` transforms to sequences and flattens one level. `filter` keeps items that pass a test.
**What are property wrappers?** Types marked `@propertyWrapper` that add behaviour to a property, such as `@State`, `@AppStorage` and `@Published`.

**What is the difference between `let` and `var`, and between `static` and `class` members?** `let` cannot be reassigned. `static` members belong to the type. `class` members also belong to the type but can be overridden by subclasses.
**What does `Codable` do?** It combines `Encodable` and `Decodable`, so a type can convert to and from formats such as JSON, with `CodingKeys` for renaming.

content.text: Memory management

items: **What is ARC?** Automatic Reference Counting. The compiler adds retain and release calls, and an object is freed when its strong count reaches zero. It is not garbage collection, so cycles are not found automatically.

**What is a retain cycle and how do you fix it?** Two objects, or an object and a closure, hold each other strongly, so neither is freed. Break the cycle with `weak` or `unowned` on one side, for example `[weak self]` in a closure.

**What is the difference between weak and unowned?** `weak` is optional and becomes nil when the object is freed. `unowned` is not optional and crashes if you use it after the object is gone, so use it only when the lifetime is guaranteed.
**Do value types need memory management?** They are copied, so they have no shared reference cycles. But a struct can contain a reference to a class, and that reference still counts.
**How do you find a memory leak?** Use the Memory Graph Debugger and Instruments Leaks, and add a `deinit` log to check that objects are freed when a screen closes.

content.text: Concurrency

items: **What is async/await?** A way to write asynchronous code that reads like synchronous code. `await` marks a point where the function may pause and let other work run.
**What is a Task?** A unit of asynchronous work. `Task { }` starts one from synchronous code and inherits the current actor and priority. Tasks can be cancelled.
**What is structured concurrency?** Child tasks, such as `async let` and task groups, live inside a parent scope and cannot outlive it, so cancellation and errors flow correctly.
**What is an actor?** A reference type that protects its mutable state by allowing one task at a time to access it. You call its methods with `await`.
**What is @MainActor?** It marks code that must run on the main thread. UI updates belong there. Views and view models that touch UI state are usually main-actor isolated.
**What does Sendable mean?** A type that is safe to pass across concurrency boundaries, such as value types of Sendable members or actors. The compiler checks it, more strictly in Swift 6 mode.

**What is the difference between GCD and Swift concurrency?** GCD uses queues and closures. Swift concurrency uses async functions, tasks and actors with compiler checks. New code usually prefers Swift concurrency, but GCD is still common in existing code.
**What is a data race and how do you avoid it?** Two threads access the same memory at once and at least one writes. Avoid with actors, immutable value types, serial queues or locks.

**How does cancellation work?** It is cooperative. Cancelling a task sets a flag. Long work should check `Task.isCancelled` or call `try Task.checkCancellation()`, and awaited system calls usually throw when cancelled.

**When do you use Combine and when async/await?** Async/await for one-time asynchronous results. Combine or AsyncSequence for streams of values over time, such as debounced search text, when you want operators like `debounce` and `combineLatest`.

content.text: SwiftUI

items: **What is the difference between @State, @Binding, @StateObject, @ObservedObject and @Observable?** `@State` is state owned by a view. `@Binding` is a two-way reference to state owned elsewhere. `@StateObject` and `@ObservedObject` are for older ObservableObject classes, owned and not owned by the view. `@Observable` is the newer macro that tracks which properties a view reads.
**Why are SwiftUI views structs?** They are cheap descriptions of the screen that SwiftUI creates and compares often. The state that must survive lives in property wrappers, not in the struct itself.

**Why does the order of modifiers matter?** Each modifier returns a new view that wraps the previous one. `.padding().background(.red)` colours the padding, while `.background(.red).padding()` does not.
**What triggers a view to redraw?** A change to state that the view's body reads. With `@Observable`, only views that read the changed property update.

**What is the difference between LazyVStack and VStack, and List and ScrollView?** `VStack` creates all children at once. `LazyVStack` creates them as needed. `List` gives rows, selection and swipe actions with efficient reuse. `ScrollView` is a plain container.
**What does `id` do in ForEach?** It identifies each item, so SwiftUI can tell which rows were added, moved or removed. Unstable ids cause lost state and wrong animations.
**How do you share data across many views?** Pass it down with initialisers or bindings, or put it in the environment with `.environment` for data many views need.

**What is the difference between `.task` and `.onAppear`?** `.task` starts an async task when the view appears and cancels it when the view disappears. `.onAppear` runs a synchronous closure and does not cancel anything.

**How do you integrate UIKit with SwiftUI?** Wrap a UIKit view with `UIViewRepresentable` or a view controller with `UIViewControllerRepresentable`, and use a Coordinator for delegate callbacks. For the other direction, use `UIHostingController`.
**How do you handle navigation in a large app?** Use `NavigationStack` with a path of value types and `navigationDestination`. Keep the path in a router object so deep links and tests can set it.

content.text: Architecture and design

items: **What is MVVM and why use it?** Model, View, ViewModel. The view model holds screen state and logic and exposes it to the view. It keeps logic out of views and makes it testable.
**What is dependency injection?** Giving an object what it needs instead of letting it create it. It lets you replace a real service with a fake in tests.
**What is Clean Architecture?** A layered design where business rules do not depend on UI or frameworks. Dependencies point inwards, using protocols at the boundaries.
**How do you split an app into modules?** With local Swift packages for features and shared code. It speeds builds, enforces boundaries and lets teams work in parallel.
**What is a repository?** An object that hides where data comes from, the network, a database or a cache, behind one interface.
**What is a singleton and what are its problems?** A single shared instance. It is convenient, but it hides dependencies and makes tests hard. Prefer injecting the object.
**How would you design an offline-first app?** Read from a local database, show it at once, sync with the server in the background, and keep a queue of changes made offline. Plan for conflicts.
**How do you design a feed with paging?** Load a page at a time, keep a cursor from the server, show a footer spinner, cache pages, handle errors per page and avoid loading the same item twice.

content.text: Data and networking

items: **SwiftData, Core Data, Realm or SQLite?** SwiftData for new iOS 17+ apps. Core Data for older versions and existing apps. SQLite libraries when you want SQL control. Choose by minimum iOS version, team knowledge and migration needs.
**How do you do a database migration safely?** Add a new model version, never edit a shipped one, test upgrades from every old version with realistic data, and have a backup plan.

**How does URLSession handle a request, and how do you cancel it?** `URLSession.shared.data(for:)` is async and throws on failure. Cancel the task and the request is cancelled. Check the HTTP status as well, because a 404 is not a thrown error.

**How do you handle authentication tokens?** Keep access tokens short-lived, store tokens in the Keychain, refresh on 401 once, serialise refreshes so many requests do not refresh together, and log out if the refresh fails.
**How do you cache images?** With the URL cache and an image cache in memory and on disk, keyed by URL. `AsyncImage` has limited control, so many apps use a library or their own cache for lists.

**What is certificate pinning?** The app accepts only a known certificate or public key for a server. It protects against some attacks but can lock users out if you rotate certificates without planning.

content.text: Security and privacy

items: **Where do you store secrets and tokens?** The Keychain. Not UserDefaults and not in source code. Secrets inside an app can be extracted, so keep real API secrets on a server.
**What does the Data Protection attribute do?** It encrypts files and ties access to the device lock state, for example complete protection while locked.
**How does Face ID work in an app?** The app calls LocalAuthentication and gets success or failure. It never sees biometric data. Add `NSFaceIDUsageDescription`.
**What is App Transport Security?** A system rule that requires HTTPS connections by default. Exceptions should be rare and narrow.
**What are the main privacy rules for the App Store?** Accurate privacy labels, usage descriptions for every permission, a privacy manifest where required, and tracking only with consent.

content.text: Testing and quality

items: **What is the testing pyramid?** Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a few UI tests. UI tests are slower and more fragile.
**How do you test code that calls the network?** Put the network behind a protocol and use a fake in tests, or use a URLProtocol stub. Tests should not depend on a real server.
**What is XCTest and what is Swift Testing?** XCTest is the long-standing framework. Swift Testing is the newer one with `@Test` and `#expect`, and it can run alongside XCTest.
**How do you test date-dependent code?** Pass the date and calendar in as parameters with defaults, so tests use fixed values.
**What is Instruments used for?** Profiling: Time Profiler for CPU, Allocations and Leaks for memory, and the SwiftUI and animation tools for rendering.

**How do you improve app launch time?** Do less before the first frame, load things lazily, avoid heavy work in `init` and at launch, reduce dynamic libraries, and measure with Instruments and MetricKit.

content.text: Release and process

items: **What is TestFlight?** Apple's beta testing service. Internal testers get builds quickly. External testers need a short beta review.

**How do you handle app signing?** Certificates and provisioning profiles prove who built the app. Automatic signing handles most cases. CI often uses a tool such as fastlane match or Xcode Cloud to manage them.
**How would you do staged rollouts?** Use phased release in App Store Connect, feature flags and remote configuration, and watch crash and metric dashboards before going to everyone.

**How do you handle a crash that only happens in production?** Read the crash reports in Xcode Organizer or a crash tool, symbolicate them, reproduce with the same OS and data, add logging, fix and release a patch, and add a test.
**What does your code review look for?** Correctness, readability, tests, naming, error handling, memory, concurrency safety, accessibility and whether the change is small enough to review.

content.text: System design questions to practise

items: Design an Instagram-like feed with images, paging, offline support and caching.
Design a chat app with delivery status, retries, push notifications and offline queue.
Design a ride or food-delivery app with live location and order tracking.
Design a notes app with sync across devices and conflict handling.
Design an analytics layer that batches events, survives crashes and respects privacy.

For each: clarify requirements, sketch the screens, choose data models, define the API, decide the caching and offline rules, think about errors, security and testing, then talk about scaling and trade-offs.

content.text: This is a starter bank of about sixty questions. Interview rounds often include a coding task, so also practise small problems in Swift on arrays, strings and dictionaries, and be ready to build a screen live. A few hundred questions exist online, but if you can explain these clearly and show projects such as the ones in this course, you are well prepared for most junior and mid-level rounds.

To rehearse with real code, build the projects in the [iOS App Development with Swift and SwiftUI course](/learn/ios-development-swift-swiftui-course). Use our [resume templates](/templates) and the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker) to turn them into clear lines on your resume, and look at the [career roadmaps](/roadmaps) for the skills each role asks for.
Your task

items: Pick 20 questions. Answer each out loud in under 30 seconds and record yourself.
Explain ARC and retain cycles using a closure from one of your own projects.
Choose one system design question and sketch the screens and data flow on paper.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain value versus reference types, ARC, async/await and @State without notes.
You have one project you can walk through in five minutes.
You can name a trade-off for every design choice you describe.

steps.say: Learn each idea well enough to say it in one sentence.
Tie it to a real example from a project you built.
Mention one pitfall or trade-off. This is what senior answers have.
In the interview, answer clearly, stop, and let the interviewer ask more.

faqs.q: How many questions do I need to learn?
faqs.a: Quality matters more than quantity. If you can explain the core ideas and show projects, you can handle new questions by reasoning.

faqs.q: What if I do not know an answer?
faqs.a: Say what you do know, explain how you would find out, and stay calm. Honest reasoning is better than a confident wrong answer.

faqs.q: Do I need to memorise code?
faqs.a: No, but you should be able to write small pieces, such as a model, a SwiftUI view with state, or an async function, without help.

quiz.q: What does weak do?
options: Becomes nil when the object is freed

Which is a value type?
